title: Chapter XXXIII

teacherSummary.text: Colonel Fitzwilliam mentions that Darcy recently saved a friend from an 'imprudent marriage.' Elizabeth realizes this means Jane and Bingley, and she weeps and stays home with a headache.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses plot in Chapter XXXIII to complicate the reader's understanding of a revelation from the colonel. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXIII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a revelation from the colonel responds to that context. writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore

Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior

writingPrompts.label: College Senior

Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD

segments.script: Today's words: tractable — easy to manage or control; lessening — making smaller or less; officious — too eager to interfere; procuring — get by special effort; hardships — a state of misfortune or affliction. “tractable”: From Middle English tractable, tractabel, from Latin tractābilis "that may be touched, handled, or managed", from tractō "take in hand, handle, manage", frequentative of trahō "draw". “lessening”: From Middle English lessenen, lasnen, equivalent to less + -en. “officious”: 15th century, from Middle English offycyous, from Latin officiōsus "kindly", from officium "service". “procuring”: From Middle English procuren, from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre "to manage, administer", from prō "on behalf of" + cūrō "to care for". “hardships”: From Middle English hardshipe, equivalent to hard + ship.

Watch for rank and condescension: Rank is displayed and enforced, above all at Rosings by Lady Catherine; Elizabeth refuses to be cowed. In this chapter: “Mr. and Mrs. Collins’s happiness; and that in speaking of Rosings and her not perfectly understanding the house, he seemed to expect” (Chapter XXXIII, paragraph 1).
